```{r, include = FALSE}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true"), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
library(bayescompR)
# chains run in parallel on this many cores; on your own machine use
# options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
options(mc.cores = 2)
```

bayescompR offers several inference engines that fail in different ways.
All of them work on the same unconstrained log density, so any model can be
fitted with any of them. This vignette describes each method, its
assumptions and its tuning parameters, and compares them on one model.

| Function | Method | Needs gradients | Target |
|----------|--------|-----------------|--------|
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "nuts")` | No-U-Turn sampler | yes | exact |
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "hmc")` | static HMC | yes | exact |
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "mala")` | Metropolis adjusted Langevin | yes | exact |
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "metropolis")` | adaptive random walk Metropolis | no | exact |
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "slice")` | slice sampling | no | exact |
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "elliptical_slice")` | generalized elliptical slice sampling | no | exact |
| `bayescomp_sample(algorithm = "fixed_param")` | no sampling: generated quantities at fixed values | no | not applicable |
| `bayescomp_smc()` | tempered sequential Monte Carlo | only with `kernel = "mala"` or `"hmc"` | consistent |
| `bayescomp_optimize()` | L-BFGS, BFGS, Newton | yes | mode |
| `bayescomp_laplace()` | normal approximation at the mode | yes | approximate |
| `bayescomp_variational()` | ADVI, mean field or full rank | yes | approximate |
| `bayescomp_pathfinder()` | Pathfinder | yes | approximate |

"Exact" means the Markov chain has the posterior as its stationary
distribution, so estimates converge to the right answer as the chains get
longer. Approximate methods converge to an approximation that can be
biased.

## A test model

Logistic regression on simulated data has a smooth, slightly correlated
posterior:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
N <- 100
X <- cbind(1, rnorm(N), rnorm(N))
beta_true <- c(-0.5, 1, -1.5)
y <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(X %*% beta_true))
code <- "
data { int N; int K; matrix[N, K] X; array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> y; }
parameters { vector[K] beta; }
model {
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  y ~ bernoulli_logit_glm(X, 0, beta);
}"
model <- bayescomp_model(code, data = list(N = N, K = 3, X = X, y = y))
```

## NUTS

The No-U-Turn sampler (Hoffman and Gelman 2014) in the form used by Stan
(Betancourt 2017): trajectories are built by doubling in both directions
until the generalized no U turn criterion holds or `max_treedepth` is
reached, and the next state is drawn from the whole trajectory with biased
progressive multinomial sampling. During warmup the step size is tuned by
dual averaging so that the mean acceptance statistic reaches `adapt_delta`
(default 0.8), and the inverse metric is estimated from the draws in a
sequence of doubling windows.

```{r}
nuts <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300,
                         seed = 1, refresh = 0)
summary(nuts)
```

Raise `adapt_delta` (for example to 0.95) when there are divergent
transitions, and use `metric = "dense_e"` for strongly correlated
posteriors.

### Controlling a run

`bayescomp_sample()` takes CmdStan's sampler arguments under the same
names:

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chains`, `iter_warmup`, `iter_sampling`, `thin` | number of chains, warmup and kept iterations, thinning |
| `seed` | one seed for the run; each chain gets its own stream, so results do not depend on `cores` |
| `cores` | chains in parallel; defaults to `getOption("mc.cores", 1)` |
| `init` | a radius (uniform on `(-init, init)` on the unconstrained scale, default 2), `0`, a named list, a list of lists (one per chain), a function, JSON or R dump file names (one per chain, recycled), or a fit whose draws start the chains |
| `algorithm` | `"nuts"`, `"hmc"`, `"mala"`, `"metropolis"`, `"slice"`, `"elliptical_slice"` or `"fixed_param"` |
| `metric`, `inv_metric` | `"diag_e"` (default), `"dense_e"` or `"unit_e"` (no metric adaptation); an initial inverse metric as a vector or matrix, or a `metric_file` JSON written by `bayescomp_write_csv(save_metric = TRUE)` |
| `step_size`, `step_size_jitter`, `max_treedepth`, `int_time` | initial step size; random jitter of it (0 to 1); NUTS tree depth limit (default 10); static HMC integration time (default 2 pi) |
| `block` | Metropolis: propose all coordinates jointly (`TRUE`, default) or one at a time |
| `adapt_engaged`, `adapt_metric`, `adapt_delta`, `adapt_gamma`, `adapt_kappa`, `adapt_t0` | step size and metric adaptation |
| `adapt_init_buffer`, `adapt_term_buffer`, `adapt_window` | warmup windows |
| `save_warmup`, `save_diagnostics` | keep warmup draws; keep momenta and gradients (CmdStan's `diagnostic_file`) |
| `refresh`, `show_print` | progress every `refresh` iterations (0 for none); output of Stan `print()` |
| `resume` | continue the chains of an earlier fit |

```{r}
fit_ctrl <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 600, thin = 2,
                             init = list(beta = c(0, 0, 0)), metric = "dense_e", adapt_delta = 0.9,
                             max_treedepth = 8, save_warmup = TRUE, seed = 2, refresh = 300)
dim(fit_ctrl$draws)        # 150 warmup and 300 sampling draws per chain are kept
fit_ctrl$step_size
fit_ctrl$inv_metric[[1]]
```

Initial values can come from a function, called once per chain, or from
data files; an adapted metric can be saved and reused:

```{r}
fit_init <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 200, iter_sampling = 200, seed = 4, refresh = 0,
                             init = function() list(beta = rnorm(3, 0, 0.5)))
init_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
bayescomp_write_data(list(beta = c(-0.5, 1, -1.5)), init_file)
metric_dir <- tempfile(); dir.create(metric_dir)
files <- bayescomp_write_csv(fit_ctrl, metric_dir, basename = "ctrl", save_metric = TRUE)
fit_file <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 1, iter_warmup = 100, iter_sampling = 200, seed = 5, refresh = 0,
                             init = init_file, metric = "dense_e",
                             inv_metric = file.path(metric_dir, "ctrl_1_metric.json"))
fit_file$inv_metric[[1]]
```

`algorithm = "fixed_param"` runs only the generated quantities, for
example to simulate data from fixed parameter values:

```{r}
sim <- bayescomp_model("
data { int N; real mu; real<lower=0> sigma; }
generated quantities { array[N] real y = normal_rng(rep_vector(mu, N), sigma); real m = mean(y); }",
  data = list(N = 20, mu = 3, sigma = 1))
fp <- bayescomp_sample(sim, algorithm = "fixed_param", chains = 1, iter_sampling = 500, seed = 1, refresh = 0)
mean(bayescomp_extract(fp, "m"))
```

### Interrupting and resuming

Pressing Ctrl-C (Esc in RStudio) stops sampling and returns what is done,
with a warning: the chains that finished or, when none did, the draws kept
so far. Chains that ran in parallel are cut to the length of the shortest
one. (Chains on a Windows socket cluster cannot be interrupted this way.)
The fit has
`interrupted = TRUE`. `resume` continues every chain of a fit from its last
draw with its adapted step size and metric, without warmup, so a short run
can be extended:

```{r, eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true") && requireNamespace("posterior", quietly = TRUE)}
more <- bayescomp_sample(model, resume = nuts, iter_sampling = 300, seed = 3, refresh = 0)
dim(more$draws)
both <- posterior::bind_draws(posterior::as_draws_array(nuts), posterior::as_draws_array(more),
                              along = "iteration")
posterior::summarise_draws(both, "mean", "rhat", "ess_bulk")
```

## Static HMC

Fixed integration time `int_time`; the number of leapfrog steps is
`int_time / step_size`. Useful for teaching and when a good trajectory
length is known.

```{r}
hmc <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300,
                        algorithm = "hmc", int_time = 2, seed = 1, refresh = 0)
```

## MALA

One Langevin step with a Metropolis correction (Roberts and Tweedie 1996):
the proposal is

$$\theta' = \theta + \tfrac{\epsilon^2}{2} M^{-1} \nabla \log p(\theta) + \epsilon M^{-1/2} z, \qquad z \sim N(0, I),$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the adapted inverse metric. MALA uses one gradient per
iteration, but it moves diffusively and can mix poorly for heavy tailed
targets. The default acceptance target is 0.574.

```{r}
mala <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 600,
                         algorithm = "mala", seed = 1, refresh = 0)
```

## Random walk Metropolis

Gaussian proposals with covariance $\epsilon^2 M^{-1}$. Because the inverse
metric is estimated from warmup draws, this is the adaptive Metropolis
algorithm of Haario, Saksman and Tamminen (2001), with adaptation confined
to warmup. `block = TRUE` (default) proposes all coordinates at once with
target acceptance 0.234; `block = FALSE` updates one coordinate at a time
with target 0.44. Metropolis needs no gradient, so each iteration is cheap,
but many more iterations are needed.

```{r}
rwm <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 1000, iter_sampling = 2000,
                        algorithm = "metropolis", metric = "dense_e", seed = 1, refresh = 0)
```

## Slice sampling

Univariate slice sampling with stepping out and shrinkage (Neal 2003)
along each direction of the Cholesky factor of the inverse metric. The
bracket width `step_size` (default 2) is in units of the metric scale. It
has no acceptance rate to tune and needs no gradient.

```{r}
slice <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300,
                          algorithm = "slice", seed = 1, refresh = 0)
```

## Tempered SMC

Sequential Monte Carlo samplers (Del Moral, Doucet and Jasra 2006) move a
population of particles through the distributions
$\pi_\beta \propto g^{1 - \beta} p^\beta$ from a normalized Gaussian
reference $g$ to the posterior $p$. Each temperature is chosen so the
effective sample size of the weights stays at `ess_threshold`; particles
are then resampled and moved with random walk Metropolis steps. SMC
explores multimodal posteriors well and returns an estimate of the log
normalizing constant, the marginal likelihood for a fully generative model.

```{r}
smc <- bayescomp_smc(model, num_particles = 300, seed = 1)
smc$log_evidence
length(smc$betas) - 1   # number of temperatures
```

The default reference is a Gaussian fitted by Pathfinder (when the model
has gradients) and the default kernel random walk Metropolis. With
`kernel = "mala"` or `"hmc"` the particles move with gradient steps, which
mix better in higher dimensions; `num_mcmc_steps` sets the moves per
temperature and `resampling` the scheme (`"systematic"`, `"stratified"`,
`"residual"`, `"multinomial"`).

```{r}
smc_hmc <- bayescomp_smc(model, num_particles = 300, kernel = "hmc", hmc_steps = 5, seed = 1)
c(metropolis = smc$log_evidence, hmc = smc_hmc$log_evidence)
```

On a mixture of two well separated normals, NUTS chains stay in the mode
where they start, while SMC finds both:

```{r}
mix <- bayescomp_model("parameters { real x; }
model { target += log_mix(0.3, normal_lpdf(x | -5, 0.5), normal_lpdf(x | 5, 0.5)); }")
s <- bayescomp_smc(mix, num_particles = 400, reference = "standard",
                   reference_scale = 8, seed = 2)
mean(bayescomp_extract(s, "x") < 0)   # exact 0.3
```

## Optimization and Laplace

`bayescomp_optimize()` finds the posterior mode (`jacobian = TRUE`, on the
unconstrained scale) or the penalized maximum likelihood estimate
(`jacobian = FALSE`, default, as in Stan). `bayescomp_laplace()` draws
from the normal approximation centered at the mode with covariance equal to
the inverse negative Hessian.

```{r}
opt <- bayescomp_optimize(model, seed = 1)
opt$par
lap <- bayescomp_laplace(model, draws = 1000, seed = 1)
```

`algorithm` chooses L-BFGS (default), BFGS or Newton's method, with
CmdStan's convergence tolerances (`tol_obj`, `tol_rel_obj`, `tol_grad`,
`tol_rel_grad`, `tol_param`). `save_iterations = TRUE` keeps every iterate,
and `bayescomp_laplace(mode = )` reuses a mode found before (it must be the
mode with `jacobian = TRUE`):

```{r}
opt_n <- bayescomp_optimize(model, algorithm = "newton", jacobian = TRUE, save_iterations = TRUE, seed = 1)
nrow(opt_n$draws)          # iterates, the optimum last
lap2 <- bayescomp_laplace(model, mode = opt_n, draws = 1000, seed = 1)
colMeans(bayescomp_draws(lap2, "beta", format = "matrix"))
```

The extra columns `log_p__` and `log_g__` hold the log density of the
model and of the approximation at each draw, for importance sampling
corrections.

## ADVI

Automatic differentiation variational inference (Kucukelbir et al. 2017)
fits a normal distribution on the unconstrained space by stochastic
gradient ascent on the evidence lower bound, with Stan's adaptive step size
sequence and convergence test on the relative change of the ELBO. Mean
field uses a diagonal covariance; full rank a dense one.

```{r}
vi <- bayescomp_variational(model, algorithm = "fullrank", seed = 1)
vi_mf <- bayescomp_variational(model, algorithm = "meanfield", seed = 1)
rbind(fullrank = apply(bayescomp_draws(vi, "beta", format = "matrix"), 2, sd),
      meanfield = apply(bayescomp_draws(vi_mf, "beta", format = "matrix"), 2, sd))
```

A variational or Pathfinder fit can also start NUTS chains near the bulk
of the posterior:

```{r}
nuts_vi <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 200, iter_sampling = 200, init = vi, seed = 6, refresh = 0)
```

ADVI's convergence criterion says the optimizer stopped, not that the
approximation is accurate: a variational family can converge perfectly to
a poor approximation. Check against MCMC.

## Pathfinder

Pathfinder (Zhang et al. 2022) runs L-BFGS, forms a normal approximation
from the L-BFGS inverse Hessian at each iterate, keeps the one with the
largest ELBO, and combines several paths by Pareto smoothed importance
resampling. It typically needs far fewer gradient evaluations than ADVI or
MCMC warmup. A Pareto $\hat k$ above 0.7 means the importance weights are
unreliable; the draws are then still good initial values.

```{r}
pf <- bayescomp_pathfinder(model, num_paths = 4, seed = 1)
pf$pareto_k
```

## Comparison

```{r}
fits <- list(NUTS = nuts, HMC = hmc, MALA = mala, Metropolis = rwm, Slice = slice,
             SMC = smc, Laplace = lap, ADVI = vi, Pathfinder = pf)
tab <- t(vapply(fits, function(f) {
  b <- bayescomp_draws(f, "beta", format = "matrix")
  c(colMeans(b), apply(b, 2, sd), time = f$time$total)
}, numeric(7)))
colnames(tab) <- c(paste0("mean[", 1:3, "]"), paste0("sd[", 1:3, "]"), "seconds")
round(tab, 3)
```

For the Markov chain methods, R-hat and the effective sample size of
`beta[3]` show how much each draw is worth:

```{r}
t(vapply(fits[c("NUTS", "HMC", "MALA", "Metropolis", "Slice")], function(f) {
  s <- summary(f, "beta[3]")
  c(rhat = s$rhat, ess_bulk = s$ess_bulk, ess_per_second = s$ess_bulk / f$time$total)
}, numeric(3)))
```

The exact methods and SMC agree to within Monte Carlo error. Laplace is
centered at the mode rather than the mean, so its means are pulled toward
zero, and ADVI gets the means right but misstates the standard deviations,
the typical failure of a variational fit. The differences grow for
hierarchical, multimodal or heavy tailed posteriors, where only the exact
methods (and SMC as the number of particles grows) remain reliable.

## Choosing a method

* Start with NUTS for any differentiable model.
* Use Pathfinder or Laplace for a quick look and for initial values.
* Use SMC for multimodal posteriors and for marginal likelihoods.
* Use Metropolis or slice sampling as independent checks, or when the log
  density is not differentiable.
* Treat ADVI and Laplace as approximations; compare with MCMC before
  relying on them.
